title: Trump's AI Executive Order Hits Key Deadline as Industry Reviews Framework
excerpt: Anthropic, OpenAI, and Alphabet have been invited to the White House to review the government's first classified benchmarking process for frontier AI models, meeting a 60-day deadline set by Trump's June cybersecurity order.
body:
• The White House met its 60-day deadline to draft a classified benchmarking process for evaluating which AI models qualify as "covered frontier models" under Trump's June 2 executive order.
  • Anthropic, OpenAI, and Alphabet have been invited to review the framework at a White House meeting hosted by National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross.
  • The order establishes a voluntary 30-day window for the government to access frontier AI models before public release — down from 90 days in earlier drafts.
  • OpenAI has already deferred its GPT-5.6 public rollout at the government's request, while Anthropic has limited the release of its Mythos model over hacking concerns.

President Donald Trump's landmark executive order on artificial intelligence has reached a pivotal moment, with the administration meeting a key August deadline to build the framework that will govern how the government evaluates the most powerful AI models before they reach the public.

The 60-Day Deadline

Signed on June 2, the executive order — formally titled "Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security" — directed federal agencies to develop two things within 60 days: a classified benchmarking process to assess the cyber capabilities of AI models, and a voluntary framework for developers to engage with the government before releasing frontier systems.

https://x.com/Serenityin24/status/2088780421202911477

The White House confirmed that security officials met the deadline, and Anthropic, OpenAI, and Alphabet received invitations to review the resulting framework at a meeting hosted by National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross, according to Barron's and The Information.

The framework's classified benchmarking process will determine which AI systems meet the threshold for designation as "covered frontier models" — a term the executive order deliberately left undefined, delegating the classification to the National Security Agency in consultation with CISA, NIST, and the Treasury Department.

Voluntary Access, Not Regulation

The order's central mechanism is a voluntary 30-day pre-release access window, allowing the government to evaluate frontier models before companies release them to trusted partners. Earlier drafts had proposed a 90-day window, but industry pushback — including from venture capitalist and former White House AI czar David Sacks — led to significant narrowing.

"Nothing in this section shall be construed to authorize the creation of a mandatory governmental licensing, preclearance, or permitting requirement for the development, publication, release, or distribution of new AI models."

— Executive Order 14409

The compromise reflects a broader tension within the administration between national security hawks alarmed by AI-enabled cyber threats and pro-innovation voices wary of regulatory overreach.

Industry Already Adapting

Even before the framework's formal rollout, major AI companies have adjusted their release strategies. OpenAI deferred a full public launch of GPT-5.6 at the government's request in late June, limiting initial access to vetted partners while the company and administration work out a repeatable process for future model releases.

Anthropic, meanwhile, has limited the release of Mythos, its most capable AI model, after discovering it has strong autonomous hacking capabilities. The discovery was a major driver behind the administration's accelerated push for oversight, reshaping what had initially been envisioned as a modest voluntary framework into a more structured engagement process.

The executive order also directs the Attorney General to prioritize prosecuting AI-enabled cybercrime under existing statutes, tasks Treasury with establishing a vulnerability coordination clearinghouse, and expands federal cyber hiring through the U.S. Tech Force.

What's Next

With the framework drafted, the focus now shifts to implementation. The industry review will determine how workable the voluntary process actually is, and whether companies beyond the biggest three will participate. The administration must also finalize its approach to state AI regulations — a separate December executive order set its own 90-day deadline for agencies to evaluate state-level AI rules, fueling an ongoing battle between federal preemption and state-level consumer protection.

For the tech industry, the August framework sets the terms of engagement with Washington on AI safety for the foreseeable future. Whether voluntary participation holds — or whether incidents force a shift toward mandatory oversight — will depend largely on what the classified benchmarking reveals about the next generation of frontier models.
